The 78723 coefficient, \(\widehat\beta_3=-0.32\), compares equally sized homes in 78723 with homes in 78731. Exponentiating it gives a fitted price about 27.5% lower in 78723.

title: 24  Modeling nonlinear relationships
text:
24.2 Polynomial regression
Polynomial regression allows for nonlinearity by adding additional powers of \(X\) to the model. A degree-\(k\) polynomial regression model has the form
\[
\widehat Y
=\widehat\beta_0+\widehat\beta_1X+\widehat\beta_2X^2+\cdots+\widehat\beta_kX^k.
\]
We treat \(X,X^2,\ldots,X^k\) just like any other predictors when we fit the model. A degree-2 polynomial is a quadratic function that can capture \(U\)-shapes (or nonlinearly increasing or decreasing relationships, depending on where the \(X\) values lie). A degree-3 polynomial is a cubic function; it can change direction twice and take more complex forms than a degree-2 polynomial. A degree-\(k\) model also includes every lower power, preserving the model’s hierarchy.
When we’re using polynomials in regression, we usually don’t care about the individual coefficients. Instead, we focus on the overall shape of the fitted curve and how well it captures the relationship between \(X\) and \(Y\).

24.2.1 Electricity load and temperature
We revisit our running nonlinear example, predicting daily electricity load in North Central Texas from the average daily temperature. Adding a quadratic term captures most of the \(U\)-shaped relationship that a straight line misses.








Figure 24.3: Daily mean electricity load against temperature in DFW during 2018. The quadratic fit captures the dominant U-shaped pattern that the straight line misses.





The fitted curve overlaid on the data suggests that we might be done — we wanted a \(U\) and we got it — but the residual-versus-fitted plot below shows we still have a violation of the linearity assumption:








Figure 24.4: Residuals versus fitted values for degree-1 (left) and degree-2 (right) ERCOT models. The quadratic removes the dominant curved pattern.





The quadratic captures most of the relationship that the line missed, but some structure remains in the residuals. In particular, for very hot or very cold days (when the fitted values are largest) we are overpredicting demand. You can actually see that in the plot of the model fit over the original data if you look closely. But you can’t miss it in the residual versus fitted plot.
Figure 24.5 shows the cubic fit and its residual plot.








Figure 24.5: The degree-3 ERCOT fit (left) and its residual-versus-fitted plot (right). The cubic makes a smaller adjustment after the quadratic captures the dominant U-shape.





The cubic changes the fitted curve only modestly, and the residual smoother still curves downward. Adding a couple more polynomial terms gets us closer to a good fit, as shown in Figure 24.6.








Figure 24.6: The degree-5 ERCOT fit (left) and its residual-versus-fitted plot (right). Most remaining departures are small relative to the original nonlinear pattern.








24.2.2 Overfitting and extrapolation
Figure 24.7 places the degree-1, degree-2, degree-3, degree-5, and degree-9 polynomials on the same figure. The quadratic captures the main U-shape, with smaller refinements from the other terms. The ninth-degree curve starts producing extra wiggles and behaves erratically at the extremes. This is characteristic of overfitting: a model that is so flexible that it can start to chase noise instead of signal.









Figure 24.7: Degree-1, degree-2, degree-3, degree-5, and degree-9 polynomial fits for 2018 DFW daily load. The quadratic captures the dominant U-shape; higher degrees add smaller bends.





High-degree polynomials are especially risky for extrapolation. At the low-temperature end of Figure 24.7, the degree-9 curve already bends back down. Figure 24.8 extends the temperature range by only eight degrees in each direction and marks the observed boundaries.








Figure 24.8: ERCOT polynomial fits extended eight degrees beyond the observed temperature range. Dashed lines mark the data boundaries; the fitted curves separate quickly outside them.





The curved models make broadly similar predictions through most of the observed range but diverge rapidly outside it. The extra flexibility that helps a high-degree model follow small in-sample bends also leaves its extrapolations controlled by the highest powers of temperature.
The “Goldilocks” degree is the one that predicts well without chasing noise. Finding it requires checking predictions on new data, which we’ll do in the next chapter.

title: 24  Modeling nonlinear relationships
text:
Appendix: Logarithms and exponentials
The natural logarithm \(\log(x)\) is defined only for \(x>0\). It is the inverse of the exponential function \(\exp(x)=e^x\), so
\[
\log(1)=0,\qquad \exp(0)=1,\qquad
\log(\exp a)=a,\qquad \exp(\log x)=x.
\]
The log and exponential functions undo one another. The last identity requires \(x>0\).
Logs turn products into sums, ratios into differences, and powers into multiplication:
\[
\log(ab)=\log a+\log b,
\qquad
\log(a/b)=\log a-\log b,
\qquad
\log(a^k)=k\log a.
\]
Each rule converts a multiplicative operation on the original scale into an additive operation on the log scale. Exponentials reverse the same move, with \(\exp(a+b)=\exp(a)\exp(b)\).
A difference between two logged values is the log of their ratio:
\[
\log(y_2)-\log(y_1)=\log(y_2/y_1).
\]
A log difference \(d\) therefore corresponds to the exact ratio \(\exp(d)\) and the exact percentage change \(100[\exp(d)-1]\%\). For small decimal changes, \(\log(1+r)\approx r\) and \(\exp(d)-1\approx d\). A 2% increase has \(\log(1.02)=0.0198\), so the approximation differs by only 0.0002. A 50% increase has \(\log(1.50)=0.4055\), so the same shortcut is much rougher.
The sign carries the direction. Positive log differences produce ratios above one, zero produces a ratio of one, and negative log differences produce ratios between zero and one. Equal positive and negative log differences correspond to reciprocal ratios: \(\exp(0.2)=1.22\) and \(\exp(-0.2)=0.82\).
Natural logs use base \(e\approx2.718\), but the base does not change the substantive pattern once coefficients are interpreted consistently. We use natural logs because their derivatives give the percentage-change approximations above and because statistical software commonly treats log as the natural logarithm.
Zero and negative values cannot be logged. Adding an arbitrary constant changes ratios and therefore changes the scientific meaning of the analysis, so it is not a generic fix for nonpositive observations.

title: 25  Measuring prediction error on new data
text:
25.1 In-sample prediction error
In Section 20.1 we used residual standard error to summarize the prediction errors from a fitted regression. Those residuals came from the same observations we used to estimate the model. They tell us how closely the model fits the data in hand.
Prediction usually asks about observations we have not seen yet. A homebuyer cares how accurately a model will value the next house, not how closely it reproduces prices that helped determine its coefficients. An electricity provider cares about tomorrow’s load. These questions concern new-data prediction error: the errors a fitted model makes on observations that played no role in fitting it.
The distinction matters whenever we compare models of different complexity. Adding terms gives a regression more ways to match the observations used to fit it, so its sum of squared residuals cannot increase. Some of that improvement may represent stable predictive information. Some may come from fitting features peculiar to one sample.

title: 25  Measuring prediction error on new data
text:
25.2 ERCOT in a new year
The ERCOT load data give us a clean first look at this problem. Daily electricity demand in North Central Texas is high on cold and hot days and lower on mild days. A line misses this U-shaped relationship, while polynomial terms let the fitted curve bend.
We fit polynomial models of degrees 1 through 20 using the 365 daily observations from 2018. These are the training observations, the data that estimate each model. We then use each fitted model to predict load for the 365 days in 2019. The two years cover comparable temperatures: every 2019 daily mean temperature falls within the range observed in 2018. High-degree models therefore cannot blame their errors on extrapolation beyond the training temperatures.
Figure 25.1 compares the root mean squared error, or RMSE, on the two years: square each prediction error, average the squares, and take the square root. The result is in megawatts, like the loads themselves. The blue series measures the errors on the 2018 observations used to fit each model. The orange series measures errors on new observations from 2019.








Figure 25.1: Prediction error for polynomial models fit to 2018 ERCOT observations. The degree-1 RMSE values are clipped at 1,250 MW and labeled with their actual values. Training RMSE falls with degree, while 2019 RMSE eventually rises.





The two error curves answer different questions. Training RMSE cannot rise with degree, because each higher-degree model retains all the lower-degree terms. Here it falls at every step, and degree 20 fits the 2018 data best among these candidates. The 2019 curve instead reaches a broad low region among the intermediate degrees and rises for the most flexible models. You may notice that the 2019 errors sit below the 2018 errors at most degrees. That reflects the years, not the models: 2019 load was easier to predict than 2018 load for every candidate here. The levels of the two curves are therefore not directly comparable. Overfitting shows up in their shapes: training error keeps falling while 2019 error eventually rises.
Degrees 5 and 6 are essentially tied for the lowest 2019 RMSE in this particular comparison, at about 610 MW; degree 6 wins by a fraction of a megawatt. That result does not establish degree 6 as the correct model for electricity demand in general. We inspected 2019 to compare the candidates, so 2019 has now helped us choose the model. A later year would be needed to evaluate the selected degree on data that remained untouched throughout model selection.
crumbs: 25  Measuring prediction error on new data

title: 25  Measuring prediction error on new data
text:
25.3 The bias-variance tradeoff
The ERCOT curves illustrate the bias-variance tradeoff. A model can predict poorly because it imposes too much structure or because it responds too strongly to the particular sample used to fit it. More flexibility reduces the first problem while increasing the second.
The degree-1 model underfits. Its straight line cannot represent the persistent U-shaped relationship between load and temperature, so its predictions have high bias. More observations would estimate that line more precisely, but they would not give it the bend it lacks.
The highest-degree models face the opposite problem. They can respond to smaller features in the 2018 observations, including features that reflect idiosyncratic variation rather than a stable relationship. A model that learns this sample-specific variation overfits. If we collected another sample and fit the model again, its smaller bends could move substantially; that sensitivity is variance.
Intermediate degrees balance these two sources of error better in this example. They are flexible enough to capture the broad U-shape but structured enough to resist smaller sample features. You can see the result in the orange curve: new-data error falls as we repair the line’s underfit, then rises when added flexibility becomes more costly than useful.
The conceptual curves in Figure 25.2 generalize this pattern. For prediction judged by squared error, expected prediction error splits exactly into three pieces: the square of the bias, the variance, and irreducible error. We state this decomposition without proof; the bias appears squared because the errors are squared before averaging. As model flexibility increases, squared bias decreases while variance increases. Irreducible error remains even for the best model because no available predictors perfectly determine the outcome. The sum of the three pieces produces a U-shaped curve for expected squared prediction error.








Figure 25.2: The bias-variance tradeoff. Greater model flexibility reduces squared bias but increases variance. Their sum with irreducible error produces a U-shaped expected squared prediction-error curve.





Polynomial degree gives us one concrete measure of flexibility. A degree-\(k\) polynomial has \(k\) terms built from its predictor and can represent more bends as \(k\) increases. For a broader regression, the number of terms gives a similar rough measure: more terms give the fitted model more ways to respond to the training sample.
The 2019 observations revealed this only after the year arrived. Model selection needs an earlier answer. We need to mimic the arrival of new observations using the data we already have.
crumbs: 25  Measuring prediction error on new data

title: 25  Measuring prediction error on new data
text:
25.4 Training and testing data
We can create a stand-in for future data by dividing the observations we have. The training data are the observations used to estimate the model. The testing data are observations set aside to measure how the fitted model predicts new cases.
The procedure has a strict order, as Figure 25.3 shows. We fit each candidate using only the training observations. We then predict outcomes in the testing data and compare them with the outcomes we held back. If you let information from a test observation enter the fitting process, it no longer supplies a new-data prediction.






Figure 25.3: A random training/testing split. The model is fit only to the training observations, then evaluated on the observations held back as testing data.



For a quantitative outcome, we can summarize the held-out errors with test RMSE:
\[
\operatorname{RMSE}_{\mathrm{test}}
=
\sqrt{\frac{1}{n_{\mathrm{test}}}
\sum_{i\in\mathrm{test}}(y_i-\widehat y_i)^2}.
\]
The test RMSE is the square root of the average squared prediction error among observations that were not used to fit the model. It uses the outcome’s original units, so a test RMSE of $150,000 means that the typical scale of the held-out errors is about $150,000.
Test RMSE is essentially the same recipe as the residual standard error from the earlier regression chapter, applied to different observations. The RSE averages squared residuals from the same data used to estimate the coefficients. Test RMSE averages squared errors for observations that played no part in the fit.
Held-out data help only when they resemble the cases where the model will be used. A random split can mimic future draws from the same population. It cannot describe performance after the population changes, such as when the housing market shifts or predictions move to a new region.

25.4.1 Random training and testing splits
The familiar Austin housing data let us see what a random split contributes. The subset contains 1,103 houses from three ZIP codes. No single time cutoff defines the prediction task here, so we randomly place 80% of the houses in training data and reserve 20% for testing.
Random assignment tends to preserve the observed mixture of large and small homes, ZIP codes, and other attributes on both sides of the split. That makes it a reasonable starting point for predicting another house from the same historical population. It does not protect us against a future market that differs systematically from these observations.
We compare the three price models in Table 25.1. The number of terms excludes the intercept and provides a rough ordering of their flexibility. The formulas stay behind the scenes because the comparison depends on what each model can represent, not on software syntax.




Table 25.1: The three Austin price models, ordered from least to most flexible.











Model
Description
Terms




Area only
Living area
1


Area + Others (Linear)
Living area, ZIP code, and ordinary listing fields
20


Expanded nonlinear

The area-only model deliberately leaves useful information out. Area + Others (Linear) adds the ZIP code, ordinary listing attributes, and an interaction that lets the area relationship differ across ZIP codes. The expanded nonlinear model adds polynomial transformations and interactions among the listing fields, raising the count from 20 to 71 terms.
The expanded nonlinear model is deliberately more flexible than the available sample seems to support. Its role is to make the cost of excess flexibility visible. Nonlinear terms and interactions are not inherently harmful; earlier chapters used both to represent relationships that a simpler model missed.
One random split gives one estimate of new-data error, and a different split can give a different answer. Figure 25.4 repeats the 80/20 procedure for 100 random splits. For each split, all three models use exactly the same training and testing houses, which makes their comparison fair.








Figure 25.4: Training and test RMSE across 100 80/20 splits of the Austin housing data. Each faint line connects results from one split, and thick lines mark medians; 2 test RMSEs above $220,000 are clipped.





Each faint path records how error changes across the three models within one split. Training RMSE falls every time. Test RMSE varies much more: in 45 of the 100 splits, the expanded nonlinear model actually beats Area + Others (Linear) on the held-out houses.
The thick lines show medians across the 100 splits. Median test RMSE falls when we move beyond area alone, then rises when we add the expanded nonlinear terms. The median therefore follows the bias-variance U-shape even though the individual paths are noisy. The annotation counts the 2 expanded-model test RMSEs above the $220,000 plotting limit rather than stretching the axis until the main pattern disappears.
A single train/test split hides this variability. Repeating the split shows the range of plausible comparisons, but an unorganized collection of splits creates another problem. Some houses may appear in testing data many times, while others may never receive a held-out prediction.

title: 25  Measuring prediction error on new data
text:
25.5 Cross-validation
Cross-validation organizes repeated splits so that every observation takes a turn in the testing data. In five-fold cross-validation, we randomly divide the rows into five approximately equal groups called folds. We then run five linked train/test comparisons.






NoteFive-fold cross-validation




Randomly divide the observations into five groups of approximately equal size.
Hold out the first group, fit the candidate model to the other four groups, and predict the held-out observations.
Repeat the fit-and-predict step until each group has served as the testing data once.
Pool the squared errors from all held-out predictions.
Take the square root of their average to obtain the cross-validated RMSE.



The five fits give every house exactly one prediction from a model that did not train on that house. Pooling the 1,103 squared held-out errors and taking their root mean produces one cross-validated RMSE for each candidate. The folds do not create five independent datasets; together, they create one complete set of out-of-sample predictions.
Figure 25.5 shows the five linked fits. Each fold supplies testing observations once and training observations four times.






Figure 25.5: Five-fold cross-validation. Each fold serves as testing data once and training data four times.



Candidate models should use the same fold assignments. Otherwise, differences in RMSE would combine differences between the models with accidental differences between their testing observations. Here each fold holds out about 20% of the Austin houses, matching the testing fraction in the earlier random splits.
Figure 25.6 shows the training and test errors from the five fits. Faint paths retain the fold-to-fold variation, while the thick paths pool squared errors over all five folds.








Figure 25.6: Training and test RMSE for the five cross-validation folds. Each faint line represents one fold; thick lines pool squared errors across all five folds.









Table 25.2: Five-fold cross-validated RMSE for the three Austin price models. Every house contributes one held-out prediction.






Model
RMSE




Area + Others (Linear)
$154,066


Expanded nonlinear
$156,703


Area only
$177,055








The pooled results select Area + Others (Linear), with a five-fold RMSE of about $154,066. The expanded nonlinear model follows at $156,703, and the area-only model trails at $177,055. The gap between the middle two models is only about $2,600, but it runs opposite to their training errors: the 71-term model fits its training rows more closely and predicts the held-out rows less accurately.
This comparison also clarifies what cross-validation can and cannot do. It gives each model the same repeated opportunities to predict observations left out of fitting, which reduces dependence on one arbitrary split. It still evaluates predictions for houses like those in this historical sample. A forecasting problem would usually preserve time order, and a problem involving new locations might hold out whole geographic groups instead of random rows.
crumbs: 25  Measuring prediction error on new data

title: 25  Measuring prediction error on new data
text:
25.6 Beyond term counting
For these Austin data, Area + Others (Linear) predicts held-out houses better than either the area-only or expanded nonlinear specification. The simpler model underfits, while the expanded model spends some of its additional flexibility on patterns that do not persist outside its training rows. In-sample fit alone points in the wrong direction.
Cross-validation gives us a defensible way to compare a short list of candidate models. The remaining problem is how to control complexity when a model begins with hundreds or thousands of possible terms. Counting terms becomes awkward at that scale, and discarding predictors one at a time is unstable.

A.2 CPS ASEC Earnings
The Annual Social and Economic Supplement (ASEC) to the Current Population Survey (CPS) is a nationally representative household survey conducted each March by the U.S. Census Bureau and Bureau of Labor Statistics. It is one of the principal federal sources for data on annual earnings, employment, and hours worked in the United States. The survey covers civilian non-institutional residents and collects detailed information on labor force participation, earnings, education, and demographics.
This dataset contains information on wages, age, education, and gender for a subsample of prime-age, full-time, full-year wage earners extracted from the Current Population Survey (CPS). The CPS is the primary source for labor market data in the U.S.; its best-known use is in estimating the unemployment rate and related statistics. It is widely used in economics research, including studies of wage determination and human capital.
Each March the CPS includes the Annual Social and Economic Supplement (ASEC), which collects detailed information on income, earnings, and work experience for the prior calendar year. The ASEC is the most comprehensive source of data on annual earnings in the U.S. This dataset was extracted from the 2023 CPS ASEC.
Resources:

CPS ASEC documentation (Census Bureau) – details about the survey design, target population, data collection, and variables available in the ASEC.
Mincer earnings function (Wikipedia) – this dataset is suitable for estimating the Mincer earnings function, a widely used model in labor economics that relates wages to schooling and experience.

Data were obtained via the cpsR R package, which queries the Census Bureau’s API and returns a tidy extract from the 2023 ASEC public-use microdata file. The underlying microdata represent civilian non-institutional respondents nationwide. No license restrictions apply to CPS public-use files; the data are freely available from the U.S. Census Bureau.

A.3 Weekly Asset Returns (2023–2025)
These data document weekly simple returns for 25 exchange-traded assets—individual equities, a sector ETF, bond ETFs, and a commodity ETF—alongside a contemporaneous weekly risk-free rate, covering the period September 30, 2023 to September 29, 2025. Prices are sourced from Yahoo Finance and converted to weekly simple returns using split- and dividend-adjusted closing prices. The dataset supports analysis of asset pricing and portfolio diversification: the companion script estimates the Capital Asset Pricing Model for each security and examines mean-variance tradeoffs across asset classes and holding-period horizons.
The data ship as two files. returns.csv contains the weekly returns and the risk-free rate only. returns_prices.csv contains the identical rows plus the weekly adjusted closing price for every asset, in columns named <ticker>_price (with SPY’s price as market_price); it supports exercises that contrast price levels with returns, such as the Ford-versus-Tesla comparison in the transformations chapter of the course notes.
Provenance. Adjusted daily closing prices were retrieved from Yahoo Finance via the tidyquant R package. The data request covers September 30, 2023 to September 29, 2025 (start_date and end_date as set in data_extract.R). The risk-free rate is proxied by the 13-week U.S. Treasury bill secondary-market yield (^IRX), converted from an annualized percentage to a weekly decimal rate by dividing by 100 and then by 52; forward-filling patches any holiday gaps in that series. Price columns in returns_prices.csv record the last available split- and dividend-adjusted daily close on or before each weekly return date, so prices and returns are aligned on the same Friday grid. Yahoo Finance terms of use restrict redistribution of raw price data; this assembled dataset is intended for educational use. A.4 Three-Asset Portfolio Series (2023–2025)
These data document weekly simple returns and adjusted prices for three exchange-traded funds—a U.S. equity market fund (SPY), an international developed-markets equity fund (EFA), and a long-term U.S. Treasury bond fund (TLT)—alongside a contemporaneous weekly risk-free rate, covering the period September 30, 2023 to September 29, 2025. The three funds were chosen for the portfolio construction material in the course notes: over this window they had nearly identical volatility but quite different mean returns, and the two equity funds are strongly correlated with each other while the bond fund is nearly uncorrelated with both. Prices are sourced from Yahoo Finance and converted to weekly simple returns using split- and dividend-adjusted closing prices.
The dataset ships as a single file, portfolios.csv, containing the weekly returns, the risk-free rate, and the aligned weekly adjusted closing prices. The rows sit on the same Friday grid as the broader weekly asset returns panel (Section A.3), so the two datasets can be joined on date; the SPY column here is the same series as that dataset’s market column.
Provenance. Adjusted daily closing prices were retrieved from Yahoo Finance via the tidyquant R package. The data request covers September 30, 2023 to September 29, 2025 (start_date and end_date as set in data_extract.R). The risk-free rate is proxied by the 13-week U.S. Treasury bill secondary-market yield (^IRX), converted from an annualized percentage to a weekly decimal rate by dividing by 100 and then by 52; forward-filling patches any holiday gaps in that series. Price columns record the last available split- and dividend-adjusted daily close on or before each weekly return date, so prices and returns are aligned on the same Friday grid. Yahoo Finance terms of use restrict redistribution of raw price data; this assembled dataset is intended for educational use. section: A.5 ERCOT Hourly Load and Temperature Panel
text:
A.5 ERCOT Hourly Load and Temperature Panel
These data were assembled to characterize the relationship between temperature and electricity demand in Texas. The panel links hourly zone-level load from ERCOT with hourly surface temperature observations from nearby weather stations, enabling temperature response functions to be estimated separately for each of ERCOT’s eight weather zones. Shaffer (2022) uses these data to examine how the load–temperature relationship changed over time, estimating the functions across rolling multi-year windows from 2002 through 2020.
Resources:

Article
Replication archive

Provenance. Load data originate from the Electric Reliability Council of Texas (ERCOT) and reflect hourly settlement-point electricity demand, in megawatts, for each of ERCOT’s eight weather zones from January 2002 through March 2021. Temperature data originate from NOAA’s Local Climatological Data (LCD) product, which reports hourly observations from Automated Surface Observing System (ASOS) and Automated Weather Observing System (AWOS) stations. NOAA LCD reports dry-bulb temperature in degrees Fahrenheit for U.S. stations; the field name HourlyDryBulbTemperature is the exact column name used in LCD exports. One representative station was selected per ERCOT weather zone. The two sources are matched on datetime and zone. Large-scale load-shed events (outages) are flagged from ERCOT operating records to allow their exclusion from estimation. All data were curated by Blake Shaffer and are archived at the replication repository above. See Shaffer (2022) for the primary citation.

Variables

Type
Unit / Range
Description

Datetime
Hourly
Timestamp of the observation, UTC. Identifies the hour of load measurement and temperature reading; used as the join key between load, weather, and outage data.

Categorical
—
ERCOT weather zone name. Eight zones: Coast (Houston), East (Tyler), Far West (Midland), North (Wichita Falls), North Central (DFW), South (Corpus Christi), South Central (Austin), West (Abilene). Used as a grouping variable; all regressions are estimated within zone.

Continuous

Hourly electricity demand for the weather zone, in megawatts. This is the outcome variable in the temperature response function regressions.

Continuous
°F
Hourly dry-bulb surface air temperature from the nearest NOAA ASOS/AWOS station. Values are in degrees Fahrenheit (NOAA LCD native units). The key predictor in all analyses; in the published paper these are converted to Celsius before modeling, but are retained in Fahrenheit in the current working script.


Outage
Binary
0 / 1
Indicator for hours affected by large-scale, operator-initiated load shedding, sourced from ERCOT operating records. Flagged events include February 2008 and February 2011. Observations with Outage == 1 are excluded from all regression estimation to avoid conflating involuntary curtailment with normal demand response. Not used in the current test.R exploratory plots but retained in the merged dataset.

A.6 LendingClub Accepted Loans
LendingClub operated an online marketplace that matched individual borrowers with investors who funded loans in small fractional shares (“notes”). To let investors screen and price loans, the company published detailed loan-level records for every funded loan — borrower credit attributes recorded at origination together with the loan’s subsequent repayment history. A.7 SAP Customer ROE
In 2005 SAP began running advertisements claiming that companies running SAP software are 32% more profitable than companies that don’t, citing a study it had commissioned from Stratascope Inc. that was never released for public scrutiny (Carr 2005). In March 2006 the technology analyst firm Nucleus Research pushed back with a research note titled “SAP customers are 20 percent less profitable than their peers.” Nucleus compiled the publicly traded companies appearing on SAP’s own web site — 81 firms — looked up each one’s return on equity (ROE) from published financial data, and compared it with the average ROE of the firm’s industry. The average across the 81 firms was 12.6%, against an industry-average benchmark of 15.7%. These data are used in the notes to estimate the mean ROE among SAP customers, to test hypotheses about both companies’ claims, and to examine what a non-random sample can and cannot support.
Resources:

Nucleus Research note G12 (PDF)
Rough Type on the ad campaign
Rough Type on the Stratascope study

Provenance. The figures are transcribed from Table 1 of Nucleus Research (2006) (Nucleus Research note G12, March 2006), which lists each company with its SAP solution(s), industry, ROE, and industry-average ROE. Nucleus reports gathering the ROE figures from Bloomberg and the industry averages from Hoovers via Yahoo! Finance. The note itself circulates today courtesy of Oracle — an SAP competitor with an obvious interest in its conclusions — though Nucleus states the analysis was conducted independently and not commissioned by any company. The one derived column, roe_diff, was added for this book.
A caution on sampling. These 81 firms are not a random sample of SAP customers: they are the publicly traded companies SAP itself chose to feature on its web site. The inference chapter leans on this fact — analyses of these data describe SAP’s showcased customers, not SAP customers in general.

section: A.9 Bloom, Han & Liang (2024) Hybrid WFH Experiment
text:
A.9 Bloom, Han & Liang (2024) Hybrid WFH Experiment
Bloom, Han & Liang (2024) ran a six-month randomized controlled trial at a Chinese technology company in 2021–2022, randomly assigning 1,612 graduate-educated employees to a hybrid work-from-home schedule (two days per week at home) or a full-time in-person control condition. The study examines whether hybrid WFH affects employee retention, job performance, promotion rates, and subjective productivity beliefs. The three datasets documented here cover the paper’s core outcomes: employee attrition, daily lines of code written by software engineers, and manager perceptions of WFH’s effect on productivity.
Resources:

Article
Replication archive

Provenance. Data were collected by the research team of Nicholas Bloom, Ruobing Han, and James Liang as part of a pre-registered field experiment conducted at a large Chinese technology firm between July 2021 and June 2022. The replication archive, including the datasets documented here, is deposited at the Harvard Dataverse (doi:10.7910/DVN/6X4ZZL) and is freely available under a Creative Commons CC BY 4.0 licence. The original article was published open-access in Nature in June 2024. See Bloom et al. (2024) for the primary citation.

Attrition
The attrition dataset (attrition.csv) contains one row per employee (n = 1,612) and records whether each individual left the firm during the study period, together with the key subgroup characteristics used to stratify comparisons in the paper.

Type
Unit / Range
Description

Discrete

Because it takes only these two values, the group mean equals the attrition rate expressed as a percentage. Outcome variable in all attrition analyses.

Categorical
Control / Treatment
Experimental assignment. “Treatment” employees followed a hybrid WFH schedule (two days per week working from home); “Control” employees worked in-person full-time. The key independent variable.


role
Categorical

Whether the employee held a managerial position. Used to stratify attrition comparisons; the paper finds that the quit-rate reduction from hybrid WFH is concentrated among non-managers.

Categorical

Employee gender. Used to stratify attrition comparisons; the paper finds a significant reduction in quit rates for female employees.

Categorical

Commute-distance indicator based on round-trip commute time, with the sample median (90 minutes) as the threshold. Employees above the median are classified as long commuters. Used to stratify attrition comparisons; the paper finds a significant quit-rate reduction for long commuters.

The productivity dataset (codelines.csv) contains one row per engineer-day observation (n ≈ 95,500) and records the daily lines of code written by software engineer employees, together with several log-transformed versions used in the analysis. Zero values are common, reflecting non-coding days.

A.11 Course Evaluations and Instructor Appearance
Do better-looking instructors get better teaching evaluations? Hamermesh and Parker (2005) collected student course evaluations for 463 course sections taught by 94 instructors at the University of Texas at Austin between 2000 and 2002, along with a measure of each instructor’s physical attractiveness: a panel of six students rated a photograph of each instructor, and the ratings were averaged and normalized. Hamermesh and Parker found that instructors rated as better looking receive systematically higher evaluations. In the regression chapters these data serve as a running multiple-regression example — in particular, whether the association between beauty ratings and evaluation scores survives adjusting for instructor age and other course and instructor characteristics.
Resources:

Article
AER package on CRAN (distributes this extract as TeachingRatings)

Provenance. The data were collected by Daniel Hamermesh and Amy Parker for Hamermesh and Parker (2005). Each row is one course section; instructor characteristics (age, gender, beauty rating, and so on) repeat across an instructor’s sections, indexed by prof. The beauty score is the average of six student panelists’ ratings of the instructor’s photograph, normalized to have mean zero across instructors (standard deviation about 0.79 in this file). This extract is the widely used teaching version of the data that circulates with Stock and Watson’s econometrics text and is distributed in the R package AER as TeachingRatings; the one column not in that distribution, generation, is a recode of age added for teaching purposes. See Hamermesh and Parker (2005) for the primary citation.

title: Appendix C — Sampling Distribution Explorer — SAP Customer ROE
text:
This app accompanies the sampling-distribution walkthrough in the chapter on sampling distributions. It simulates the population of 30,000 ROE values described there, so you can redraw samples at will. Each draw records the mean ROE of \(n\) companies — and \(n\) is yours to change, unlike the study’s fixed 81. The means accumulate into the sampling distribution of the sample mean. Checkboxes add the normal approximation and a 95% confidence interval whose coverage you can track across thousands of samples.
The app runs in your browser and takes a few moments to start.

title: Appendix D — Bootstrap Explorer — SAP Customer ROE
text:
This app accompanies the section on the bootstrap. It shows the 81 firms of the Nucleus sample and resamples them with replacement, one resample at a time. Repeated firms light up and omitted firms grey out, so each press shows exactly what resampling with replacement does to a real sample. The resample means accumulate into the bootstrap approximation to the sampling distribution of the sample mean, with the CLT normal approximation available for comparison.
The app runs in your browser and takes a few moments to start.

title: Appendix E — Bagging Explorer — Averaging Regression Trees
text:
This app shows bagging — averaging many regression trees — in action. The data are 100 simulated points from a curved relationship between one predictor \(x\) and a response \(y\). Each press draws a resample of the 100 points with replacement, fits a regression tree to it, and adds that tree to the ensemble average. One tree wiggles; the average of many settles toward the shared structure. An out-of-bag error curve tracks prediction error on the points each tree never saw, and it flattens quickly as trees accumulate.
The app runs in your browser. It loads a full R runtime plus the rpart package, so give it up to half a minute to start.
